name: Multi-Modal Material Identity Integration and Cross-Modal Prediction
short_description: Brain constructs unified material percept from visual, haptic, acoustic, olfactory channels; cross-modal prediction violations produce inauthenticity signals
structural_pattern: The brain constructs a unified material percept from parallel sensory channels: visual (grain, color, reflectance, texture), haptic (roughness, compliance, temperature), acoustic (impact sound, resonance, absorption), and olfactory (VOC signature). Each channel generates predictions about the other channels based on learned material-identity associations. Contact that CONFIRMS these cross-modal predictions produces processing fluency and material authenticity. Contact that VIOLATES them produces cross-modal PE and material inauthenticity — the 'something is off' experience of veneer, laminate, or deceptive surface treatments.
higher_order_principle: Extension of AX5 (cross-modal congruence) to material identity. MAT3 specifies which material properties are predicted by which sensory channels, what physical parameters determine congruence vs. violation, and how multi-channel convergence produces the qualitative sense of 'real material' vs. 'fake material'.

authenticity_gradient.high_authenticity: All modalities confirm each other (solid wood throughout)
authenticity_gradient.fake: Major multi-channel discrepancy (printed film on steel)

causal_links.evidence_base: Vision dominates material identification (Klatzky & Lederman, 2010). Visual recognition activates material category and generates predictions for ALL other modalities.
Spence & Gallace (2011): visual-haptic incongruence slows material categorization and reduces confidence.
Low cross-modal PE → 'real' material, fluency, positive affect. High cross-modal PE → 'fake' material, disfluency, negative affect.
Sustained material authenticity → cumulative trust in built environment → component of Zumthor's 'atmosphere'.
Light-material interaction: narrow-band illuminants can distort material appearance → false cross-modal predictions. Connects to L4.

scope_conditions: Applies to all materials visible and/or contactable in the space
Prediction strength scales with material familiarity — well-known materials generate strong predictions
Architectural context modulates acceptability — unexpected properties may be read as artistic intention in a museum but as fakeness in a home
Veneers and laminates are the canonical case of cross-modal violation
moderators: Cultural familiarity: cross-modal predictions are learned
Lighting quality: broadband light preserves visual material identity (scope from L4)
Contact opportunity: in no-touch spaces, only visual-acoustic interaction operates
Price/quality expectations: occupants of high-end spaces have stronger authenticity expectations
Aging and patina: materials that age gracefully develop richer cross-modal signatures

interactions.nature: MAT3 is the material-specific instantiation of AX5.
T1 captures visual-grain dimension of natural material perception. MAT3 embeds T1 as one visual channel.
L4 determines how lighting affects material color appearance. Poor color rendering → distorted visual identity → elevated MAT3 PE.
MAT1 provides affective dimension of haptic contact. MAT3 provides predictive dimension: brain predicts CT response based on visual material identity.
